description.summary: A male nightmare spirit of German and Austrian folklore that sits on the chests of sleepers, causing oppressive dreams, sleep paralysis, and breathlessness; closely related to the female Mara of broader Germanic tradition.
description.full: The Alp (also Alb, plural Alpen or Albe) is a male nightmare-bringing spirit central to German and Austrian folklore. Witnesses and folk accounts describe a small, often unseen male figure that climbs onto a sleeper at night and presses on the chest, causing the sensation of being crushed (Alpdruck, 'elf-pressure'), suffocation, and immobility. The Alp is associated with the Tarnkappe, a 'concealment cap' that grants invisibility, and with shapeshifting into cats, pigs, dogs, snakes, birds, and white butterflies. Beliefs about its origin vary: in some traditions Alps are stillborn children, the unbaptized dead, or are born to women under particular conditions (a child with eyebrows that meet, or born in a caul). The Alp shares a Common Germanic root with the English word elf, and the term 'Alpdruck' is a clear cognate of English 'nightmare' (and the noun 'Alp' was eventually superseded by 'Albtraum' in modern German). Modern medicine and folklore studies recognise the experience underlying Alp belief as sleep paralysis with hypnagogic hallucination, a cross-cultural pattern documented under names such as the Mara, the Old Hag, the Pisadeira, and the kanashibari.

etymology.origin: The German Alp / Alb derives from Common Germanic *albiz, the same root as English 'elf' and Old Norse 'álfr'. The compound 'Alpdruck' literally means 'Alp-pressure'.
etymology.meaning: Originally a generic term for an elf or supernatural being; specialised in German into the chest-pressing nightmare spirit.
etymology.first_use: Old High German alp is attested from at least the 9th century; modern Alp / Albtraum sense becomes standard by the 18th century.

related_phenomena.name: Mara
related_phenomena.description: Female chest-pressing nightmare spirit of broader Germanic / Scandinavian tradition

features.description: A magical hat that grants invisibility; said to be worn by the Alp at all times
Typically described as a small male figure, though invisible during attacks
A gaze that brings illness or misfortune

physical.morphology: Primarily known by effect rather than direct visual appearance; when seen, typically as a small, hat-wearing male figure or as one of its animal disguises.

abilities.description: Transforms into cats, pigs, dogs, snakes, birds, or white butterflies
The concealment cap renders the Alp unseen
Sits on the sleeper's chest, producing breathlessness and immobility
Petty malice, including souring of stored milk and the tangling of human or horse hair into 'elf-knots' (Alpzopf)
Said to ride horses through the night, leaving them sweating and tangled

patterns: Targets sleepers, especially women and children

range.description: Alp belief is concentrated in German-speaking Europe (Germany, Austria, German-speaking Switzerland) with overlapping traditions in neighbouring regions sharing the broader Mara complex.

first_recorded.source: Old High German charms and glosses

peak_activity_periods.description: Documentation by Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm in 'Deutsche Mythologie' and the Kinder- und Hausmärchen

origins.cultural_roots: Rooted in Common Germanic 'elf' beliefs, with the German tradition specialising the Alp into the chest-pressing nightmare-bringer.
origins.earliest_accounts: Old High German charms invoking protection from elves; later medieval medical and demonological treatises name the Alp as the agent of nocturnal suffocation.
origins.folklore_connections: Continuous with the Scandinavian Mara, the English night-hag, and the broader European incubus / succubus tradition.

timeline.event: Old High German texts invoke protection against alp / alb
Jacob Grimm publishes 'Deutsche Mythologie', systematising Alp / Alb beliefs
timeline.significance: Foundational text of German folkloristics on the Alp

timeline.event: Henry Fuseli paints 'The Nightmare', depicting an incubus-like figure on a sleeper's chest
timeline.significance: Iconic visual representation of the Alp / Mara complex in Western art

history.modern_era: In contemporary Germany the noun 'Alp' has largely been replaced by 'Albtraum' for ordinary nightmares; the folkloric Alp survives in heritage collections, regional storytelling, and academic folkloristics. The phenomenology underlying Alp belief is understood medically as sleep paralysis with hypnagogic hallucination.

documentary.name: Deutsche Mythologie (Grimm, 1835)
documentary.description: Jacob Grimm's collation of Germanic mythological and folk-belief material, including chapters on Alp / Alb / Mar and the Tarnkappe.
documentary.analysis: A foundational primary scholarly source for Alp folklore.

paranormal.name: Spirit / demonic entity
paranormal.description: Folk-belief frames the Alp as an actual nocturnal entity that physically attacks sleepers, sometimes identified with the souls of unbaptized dead or stillborn children.
evidence_cited: Witness reports of chest pressure and visual presence

scientific.name: Sleep paralysis with hypnagogic hallucination
scientific.description: The Alp experience corresponds to REM-sleep atonia persisting briefly into wakefulness, accompanied by chest-pressure sensation and hallucinated presence.
evidence_cited: Cross-cultural recurrence of chest-pressing nightmare figures (Mara, Old Hag, Pisadeira, Kanashibari)

skeptical.name: Cultural framing of common physiological event
skeptical.description: The Alp is the German cultural interpretation of a universal physiological experience, requiring no entity-level explanation.
evidence_cited: Hufford, The Terror That Comes in the Night (1982)

stories: Tales of the Tarnkappe (in connection with the Nibelungenlied's Alberich)
Folk warnings and protective charms collected by the Brothers Grimm
folklore.beliefs: Protective practices include placing iron horseshoes or broomsticks at the threshold, leaving shoes facing the door, plugging keyholes, and keeping a mirror or steel object near the sleeper.

literature: Hufford, David (1982), The Terror That Comes in the Night
film_tv: Henry Fuseli, 'The Nightmare' (1781) — visual representation of the chest-pressing nightmare figure

researchers.name: Jacob Grimm
researchers.contribution: Systematic documentation of Germanic folklore including Alp

researchers.name: David J. Hufford
researchers.contribution: Cross-cultural study of sleep-paralysis 'old hag' / Alp experiences

research.ongoing_studies: Folklore departments and sleep-medicine groups continue cross-cultural research on the Alp / Mara / Old Hag complex.

sources.title: The Terror That Comes in the Night: An Experience-Centered Study of Supernatural Assault Traditions
